In 2022-23, two Indian states paid women a regular cash transfer with no strings on how it’s spent. In 2025-26, 12 states budgeted ₹1,68,040 crore for it.

That’s 0.5% of GDP, built in three years, mostly without anyone calling it a basic income.

Thanks for reading Anupam’s Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Economic Survey puts these transfers at 11-24% of monthly income for women daily wage workers. That’s real money in the hands of people budgets usually miss.

Now the constraint. PRS found six of the 12 states budgeted a revenue deficit. Take the transfer out of Karnataka’s numbers, and a deficit of 0.6% of GSDP becomes a surplus of 0.3%.

So part of this is borrowed money paying for monthly spending. It is a nightmare for textbook economists. frown. I’d be worried only if the transfer does not lift demand enough; the jury is still out on this.

Here’s what worries me more, and it’s a data problem.

Maharashtra has removed over 92 lakh names from Ladki Bahin. Some were surely ineligible. Some were probably women who got stuck in the process, and a failed verification (e-KYC) looks exactly like a saving on the budget line.

A simple transparency rule could be more helpful, i.e. publish every deletion by reason and by district, and let a woman who failed e-KYC come back without reapplying.

If your state cut its list, could you find out who was dropped and why?
